title: Alakshmi Out, Lakshmi In
hook: a stove scrubbed at 10pm before Diwali, and a hymn that gives misfortune a face and shows it the door
tomorrow: is Lakshmi only the goddess of money?

segments.voice: Yesterday named her tree, the bilva, born from her own tapas: even fortune grows from disciplined heat. Today, the hymn meets the one it wants gone.

A home can have a corner that sags. The junk drawer that won't close. The sink that's been full since Tuesday. The pile of mail nobody wants to open. None of it is a disaster. But walk into a room like that when you're already tired, and something heavy can settle on the shoulders. The Sri Sukta has a name for that heaviness, and it isn't shy about it. A few lines ago the singer asked for misfortune to be gone. Today the hymn describes her, and then rolls up its sleeves.
screen: `THE DRAWER THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `THE SINK FULL SINCE TUESDAY.` → `A NAME FOR THE HEAVINESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Hunger and thirst and grime, the elder one, Alakshmi: I drive her away. Non-prosperity, lack, all of it, push it out of my house. Alakshmi is the hymn's word for misfortune, the shadow of Lakshmi. And look at what she's made of. Not curses or monsters. Hunger. Thirst. Dirt. The ordinary signs of a house that's struggling. Then the word elder. In later tellings, tradition makes Alakshmi Lakshmi's older sister, and some honor her as a goddess in her own right, as Jyeshtha, the elder. The hymn itself just gives the word and moves on. Now the grammar, because it's the surprise. The first verb is I. I drive her away. For once, the singer isn't only asking; he takes part. Then he turns back to the goddess: you, push the rest out of my house. Many teachers read a partnership in that: the person sweeps, and grace finishes the work. And here is a big reason Hindu families clean so hard before Diwali. Scrubbing, whitewashing, throwing out what's broken. Many say it plainly: Alakshmi out, Lakshmi in. In parts of Bengal, families even see a small figure of Alakshmi out of the house before Lakshmi is worshipped. Fortune in this hymn lives in a household, and a household has dishes and floors and a pantry to keep. Misfortune here isn't a fate from the sky. It has a face and an address, and the family is willing to show it the door, before the lamps are lit and the guest comes in.
screen: `HUNGER, THIRST AND GRIME.` · `ALAKSHMI, THE ELDER ONE.` · `I DRIVE HER AWAY; YOU FINISH IT.` · `WHY FAMILIES SCRUB BEFORE DIWALI.` · then, large: `ALAKSHMI OUT, LAKSHMI IN.`

segments.voice: In your mind, find the corner of your home that sags, the drawer, the sink, the pile, and look at it honestly, without scolding yourself. Then picture it clear, one surface empty and wiped, and breathe there; after this, clear it for real, the way families do before Diwali. If you pray, you can ask the goddess, or God, for help with the part you can't do alone; if you don't, simply decide which small part is yours.
The Sri Sukta. A hymn that names Alakshmi, the elder one, made of hunger, thirst and grime, and says: I drive her away; you push the rest out of my house.
Your line: Alakshmi out, Lakshmi in. You do your part, and grace finishes the work. Rest well.

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verses 7–8 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)

notes: Verse 8 paraphrased: kṣutpipāsāmalāṃ jyeṣṭhām alakṣmīṃ nāśayāmy aham / abhūtim asamṛddhiṃ ca sarvāṃ nirṇuda me gṛhāt. nāśayāmi is first person ('I destroy / I drive away'); nirṇuda is imperative. The script rests on this shift; confirm the reading.
Verse 7 (upaitu māṃ devasakhaḥ kīrtiś ca maṇinā saha) mentioned briefly; 'devasakha' as Kubera is a traditional reading, attributed to tradition. Confirm.

Alakshmi as Lakshmi's elder sister and Jyeshtha as a goddess in her own right are later Puranic and regional traditions, attributed to 'later tradition'. Jyeshtha glossed 'the elder' (lexical). Confirm.
